planting.note: Cold-moist stratify fresh acorns 60-90 days or sow directly in fall 1 inch deep in gravelly, well-drained soil; this red-oak-group species germinates the following spring and grows slowly for its first several years in the canyon bottoms and sheltered slopes it favors.

directions: Chisos Red Oak is the signature deciduous canopy tree of the Davis Mountains, Chisos Mountains, and Guadalupe Mountains sky-island canyons, where it forms the shaded oak-pine woodland overstory alongside pinyon and ponderosa pine at 4,500-7,500 feet elevation. It tolerates considerably more shade than lowland Texas red oaks and colors brilliant scarlet to maroon in fall, a rare sight in the Trans-Pecos. Plant in rocky, sharply drained soil on a protected slope or canyon bottom; it is highly drought tolerant once established but appreciates occasional deep summer water during extended dry spells. Give it a permanent site with room for a broad crown, since like most oaks it resents transplanting once its taproot is established.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns promptly after fall collection, 1 inch deep in gritty, well-drained soil; viability drops quickly in storage, and seedlings establish best with light shade and a cool, humid microsite the first year or two.

directions: Silverleaf Oak is a defining midstory tree of Madrean pine-oak woodland, found in the Davis and Chisos Mountains of West Texas, sky islands of southeastern Arizona and New Mexico, and south into the Sierra Madre Occidental, often growing as an understory associate beneath Apache and ponderosa pine. Its narrow, willow-like evergreen leaves have a dense white-silver felt on the underside that flashes distinctively in canyon breezes, giving the species its common name. It is genuinely shade-adapted compared to most oaks and thrives on steep, rocky, north-facing canyon slopes with excellent drainage, needing little water once its root system is established beyond an occasional deep soak during summer drought. Use it as a specimen understory or screening tree in a woodland garden that mimics its native canyon habitat.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Cold-moist stratify seed 60-90 days before spring sowing, or sow outdoors in fall so winter chilling breaks dormancy naturally; this high-elevation five-needle pine grows slowly and benefits from light shade and steady moisture while young.

directions: Southwestern White Pine is the characteristic high-elevation conifer of sky-island pine-oak woodland, reaching its easternmost populations on the upper slopes of Mount Livermore in the Davis Mountains and in the Guadalupe Mountains, with the main range continuing through the mountains of southern New Mexico, Arizona, and the Sierra Madre Occidental. Unlike the lowland pinyons of the surrounding desert, it occupies cool, moist, often north-facing canyon heads and ridges above about 6,500 feet, frequently growing beside Douglas fir and Gambel oak. Plant in well-drained but not droughty soil with some afternoon shade, especially while young, and provide supplemental water during the first several years and in extended dry spells thereafter. Its soft, blue-green needles in bundles of five and large resinous cones make it a distinctive specimen conifer for a high-elevation or northern woodland garden setting.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow cleaned samaras in fall after a 30-60 day cold-moist stratification, or set out container stock in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; this small evergreen ash is slow to establish but very low-maintenance once rooted into a rocky canyon microsite.

directions: Littleleaf Ash is a small multi-trunked evergreen tree or large shrub of dry limestone canyon washes and rocky slopes across the Chihuahuan Desert sky islands, including Big Bend, the Davis Mountains, and adjacent Mexico, and it is unusual among ashes in being genuinely drought tolerant and nearly evergreen in mild winters. Its tiny, dense, aromatic leaflets give it a fine, airy texture well suited to small courtyard gardens, screening, or as a large shrub beneath taller canyon oaks. Plant in full sun to dappled shade on sharply drained, limestone-derived soil and water only occasionally once established; it tolerates reflected heat and rocky, shallow soils that defeat most other small trees. Light pruning can shape it into a single-trunk patio specimen or left unpruned as a dense multi-stemmed privacy screen.

planting.note: Sow cleaned seed on the soil surface in spring once nights stay above 55F, or plant container stock after frost; it needs no pretreatment to germinate but seedlings are frost-tender for their first winter and should be protected or planted out only after that risk has passed.

directions: Chisos Rosewood is the narrow-leaved, more cold-tender counterpart of Arizona rosewood, restricted in the United States to canyon woodland of the Chisos Mountains and the adjacent Sierra del Carmen of Coahuila, where it grows as a dense evergreen shrub among oaks on rocky slopes. Clusters of small white flowers cover the shrub in corymbs in late spring, attracting pollinators, followed by leathery seed capsules, while the narrow, leathery, finely toothed leaves give it a refined, willow-like texture distinct from its broader-leaved relative. Plant in full sun to light shade on well-drained, rocky or caliche soil and water only sparingly once established; it is markedly more sensitive to hard freezes than Vauquelinia californica, so site it with some overhead or western protection in the colder parts of its growable range. It makes an excellent unclipped screen or specimen shrub in a Chihuahuan Desert canyon-themed planting.

planting.note: Surface-sow the tiny seed in spring and keep lightly moist, since it needs light to germinate and should not be buried; established shrubs are easiest to propagate from softwood cuttings taken in early summer.

directions: Texas Mock Orange is a deciduous shrub restricted to shaded limestone canyon walls and talus slopes of the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos canyon country, often rooting directly into rock crevices on north-facing cliffs alongside columbine and canyon species. Its fragrant, four-petaled white flowers open in mid-to-late spring and are among the showiest of the native mock oranges, drawing bees and butterflies to otherwise shaded canyon niches. Plant in part shade on rocky, well-drained soil and give it a bit more moisture than typical Trans-Pecos natives, since it naturally grows where canyon seeps and runoff provide extra humidity; full sun scorches the foliage. Use it tucked among boulders or beneath taller canyon trees where its arching habit and spring bloom can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat by nicking or soaking in hot water, then cold-moist stratify about 30 days before spring sowing; pretreated seed germinates readily and young plants grow quickly, often suckering to form thickets.

directions: New Mexico Locust is a thorny, thicket-forming small tree of canyon bottoms and the transition margin between pine-oak woodland and higher montane forest across the sky-island ranges of West Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and the Sierra Madre, often colonizing disturbed slopes and drainage edges after fire. In late spring it produces pendulous clusters of fragrant, wisteria-like pink to lavender pea flowers that are a significant early-season nectar source, followed by flattened seed pods. Plant in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil; it tolerates both summer monsoon moisture and extended dry spells once established, and its suckering habit makes it useful for erosion control on canyon slopes but means it needs room to spread or occasional root-pruning in a garden setting. Give it an open site away from foot traffic, since the stout paired thorns on new growth are sharp.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
